records.role_summary: Protein is an essential macronutrient needed to build, repair, and maintain tissues, muscles, hormones, and enzymes throughout the body.
records.title: Protein and Amino Acids — Dietary Reference Intakes

records.role_summary: Carbohydrates are the body's primary energy source, fueling the brain, central nervous system, and physical activity. Quality sources include whole grains and dietary fiber.
records.title: Carbohydrates — Dietary Reference Intakes

records.role_summary: Dietary fats provide concentrated energy, support cellular structure, help absorb fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K), and supply essential fatty acids.
records.title: Dietary Fats — Dietary Guidelines for Americans

records.role_summary: Dietary fiber supports digestive health, promotes bowel regularity, aids in blood sugar and cholesterol management, and increases meal satiety.
records.title: Dietary Fiber on the Nutrition Facts Label

records.role_summary: Calories measure the energy provided by food and beverages. Energy balance—matching calories consumed to energy expended—is fundamental to health maintenance.
records.title: Calories on the Nutrition Facts Label

records.role_summary: Total sugars include both naturally occurring sugars (such as in milk and fruit) and sugars added during processing or preparation.
records.title: Total Sugars on the Nutrition Facts Label

records.role_summary: Added sugars are sugars and syrups incorporated into foods during processing or preparation. Moderating added sugars helps maintain nutrient-dense dietary patterns.
records.title: Added Sugars on the Nutrition Facts Label

records.role_summary: Serving size on a nutrition label reflects a standardized amount typically consumed, not a dietary recommendation. All listed nutrient amounts apply specifically to that serving.
records.title: Serving Size on the Nutrition Facts Label

records.role_summary: Per 100 g or 100 ml values provide a normalized nutrient density standard, enabling direct nutritional comparison across different products regardless of serving or package size.
records.title: Guidelines on Nutrition Labelling

names: how should i read a nutrition label
how to read a nutrition label
records.role_summary: To read a nutrition label effectively: start with the serving size and servings per container, check total calories, monitor nutrients to limit (saturated fat, sodium, added sugars), and check nutrients to get enough of (fiber, vitamins, and minerals).
records.title: How to Understand and Use the Nutrition Facts Label

records.role_summary: Vitamin A has established roles in normal vision, immune function, cellular communication, growth and development.
records.title: Vitamin A and Carotenoids — Health Professional Fact Sheet

records.role_summary: Vitamin C is required for collagen biosynthesis, has antioxidant functions, supports immune function, and improves absorption of nonheme iron.
records.title: Vitamin C — Health Professional Fact Sheet

records.role_summary: Vitamin D supports calcium absorption and maintenance of bone health; a label value alone cannot establish vitamin D status.
records.title: Vitamin D — Health Professional Fact Sheet

records.role_summary: Calcium contributes to the structure of bones and teeth and participates in muscle function, nerve transmission, blood clotting, and other physiological processes.
records.title: Calcium — Health Professional Fact Sheet

records.role_summary: Iron is a component of hemoglobin and supports oxygen transport; an individual food-label value cannot diagnose iron status or anemia.
records.title: Iron — Health Professional Fact Sheet

records.role_summary: Potassium has roles in cellular, muscle, and nerve function and in blood-pressure regulation; personal intake advice depends on health and medication context.
records.title: Potassium — Health Professional Fact Sheet

records.role_summary: Zinc supports many cellular processes, including immune function and wound healing; food-label evidence does not establish zinc status.
records.title: Zinc — Health Professional Fact Sheet

records.role_summary: High-sodium dietary patterns are associated with raised blood pressure; one product or diary entry is not a diagnosis or a complete diet assessment.
records.title: Sodium reduction
